ideas.title: The Only Tech IPO Where Growth Makes the Math Worse
ideas.trend: OpenAI filed confidentially for IPO on May 22 targeting $852B-$1T valuation. Q1 2026 data: -122% operating margin, losing $1.22 per dollar of revenue. Cash burn projected to peak at $47B in 2028 before any path to positive cash flow.
ideas.consensus: OpenAI is the defining growth story of the AI era; the IPO prices in a path to profitability as scale eventually reduces compute costs.
ideas.angle: OpenAI's cost structure moves in the wrong direction at scale. More capable models cost more per inference query. Gross margin compressed from 40% to 33% as revenue quadrupled. The IPO is a capital-raising vehicle, not a graduation moment — the company needs $50-80B in fresh capital just to reach 2030.

content_pack.x_longform:
The $1 trillion IPO thesis for OpenAI depends on a company where scale eventually fixes the unit economics. The Q1 2026 numbers run in the opposite direction.

Revenue: $5.7 billion in Q1. Operating margin: negative 122%. For every dollar OpenAI generated, it spent $2.22 to produce it. Where's Your Ed At broke down the filing numbers this week: total losses of roughly $6.95 billion on $5.7 billion in revenue, stripped of stock-based compensation.

The burn projections are the part worth sitting with.

2026 cash burn: $17 billion. 2027: $35 billion. 2028: $47 billion peak. To reach positive cash flow before 2030, OpenAI needs between $50 billion and $80 billion in additional capital, on top of the $122 billion already committed. The IPO is the first public tranche of that pipeline.

The standard software IPO thesis runs: burn early, achieve scale, margins expand, profit emerges. Amazon ran negative margins for a decade. Netflix borrowed its way to content scale. Both eventually printed cash because their cost structures benefit from utilization pooling. A cloud server provisioned for one customer serves a second at near-zero incremental cost. A streaming library pays for itself once and streams indefinitely.

OpenAI's inference does not work that way.

Each generation of model is more capable and more expensive per query. GPT-4 cost less to run than o3. Better answers require proportionally more compute at inference. There is no utilization pooling. Every question into ChatGPT is a direct, proportional compute expense. The-Decoder confirmed gross margins compressed from 40% in 2024 to 33% in 2025 even as revenue quadrupled. Scale made the margin worse.

ChatGPT user growth stalled in parallel. The product averaged 905 million weekly users in Q1, short of the one-billion target OpenAI had set for 2025. Converting free users to paid subscriptions is the only structural margin lever available. That conversion is not accelerating.

The infrastructure comparisons are worth making directly.

AWS reached positive operating income in 2015 on shared compute, utilization scale, and amortized fixed costs. Google Cloud turned profitable in 2023 using the same structural logic. Microsoft Azure runs at roughly 22% operating margin today. All three benefit because compute capacity, once provisioned, serves multiple customers. An idle server is an asset. An unanswered ChatGPT query is not a cost center, but each answered query carries a full compute expense.

The Deployment Company JV, a $10 billion vehicle with 19 investors, raised $4 billion in fresh capital. At 2026 burn rates, that covers approximately 12 weeks of operations. The pipeline needs to refill every quarter at increasing volumes.

Cisco held the global market cap lead in 2000 with real margins, real moats, and a genuine monopoly on networking hardware. The stock dropped 86% when growth slowed. Cisco had better unit economics at peak than OpenAI has today.

The S-1 will model a path to profitability. It will show large TAMs and strong revenue compounding. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley will price it accordingly.

Scale is the problem. The S-1 needs to explain why the next four quarters look different from the last four.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Negative 122%. That is OpenAI's operating margin for the first quarter of 2026, and it is the number doing all the work in the IPO story.

The company generated $5.7 billion in revenue and lost roughly $6.95 billion to do it, even stripping out stock-based compensation. Where's Your Ed At newsletter broke this down after the confidential filing this week. Cash burn projections go from $17 billion in 2026 to $47 billion in 2028. To reach positive cash flow by 2029, OpenAI needs between $50 and $80 billion in additional capital. The IPO is the first tranche.

The cost structure is the detail worth dwelling on. Usually, revenue growth in technology expands margins. AWS prints cash today because a 2012 infrastructure investment still serves customers in 2026. OpenAI's inference does not compound that way. Each new model generation costs more per query to run than the last. Gross margins went from 40% to 33% even as revenue quadrupled.

I am not yet sure whether there is a structural shift coming that breaks this pattern. There may be a compute efficiency breakthrough that collapses inference costs fast enough to outrun demand growth. But through Q1 2026, scale moved in the wrong direction. The S-1 will argue otherwise. It will need to make a compelling case for why the next four years look different from the last four quarters.

ideas.title: Modal Runs the Plumbing Every AI Company Rents
ideas.trend: Modal Labs raised a $355M Series C at $4.65B valuation on May 21, quadrupling from $1.1B. Revenue grew 5x from $60M to $300M ARR in 8 months, making it the fastest-growing company in AI infrastructure.
ideas.consensus: The AI infrastructure story is about compute, GPUs, and hyperscaler capex. The model race is the primary value driver.
ideas.angle: The fastest-growing company in the AI stack runs inference, not models. Modal's 5x revenue growth in 8 months outpaces every model company's trajectory. Inference infrastructure monetizes before the application layer — the same pattern that made AWS and Qualcomm the quiet winners of prior tech cycles.

content_pack.x_longform:
Modal runs the plumbing that every AI company needs and almost none wants to build.

Revenue went from $60 million annualized to $300 million in eight months. Valuation from $1.1 billion to $4.65 billion in the same window, per SiliconAngle. General Catalyst and Redpoint led the Series C.

The pitch is serverless GPU compute for AI inference. No server management. No provisioning. Pay per use, ship faster. As the number of AI models in production grows, inference demand grows with it regardless of which model wins any benchmark.

The benchmark wars produce the headlines. Fireworks, Together, Baseten, and Modal compete for the inference layer beneath them. One of those four grew 5x in eight months.

The inference layer cashes the checks.
content_pack.x_thread:
T1: Modal runs the GPU infrastructure that every AI company needs and almost none wants to operate. $60M to $300M ARR in 8 months. That number is worth paying attention to.

T2: Revenue: $60M annualized in September. $300M today. Valuation: $1.1B to $4.65B in the same window. General Catalyst and Redpoint led the Series C, per SiliconAngle.

T3: The pitch is simple: rent GPU compute for AI inference. No server management, no provisioning. Pay per use. As AI models in production multiply, the inference bill grows with every one of them.

T4: The historical pattern here is consistent. In the early cloud era, AWS grew faster than most software companies built on top of it. In mobile, Qualcomm printed better numbers than most app developers. The infrastructure layer monetizes before the application layer.

T5: Modal competes with Fireworks, Together, Baseten, and hyperscaler inference endpoints. The category is crowded. But $60M to $300M in 8 months is a product signal, not just a category signal.

T6: The model race gets all the coverage. Every benchmark release, every lab announcement, every valuation round for frontier AI companies. Meanwhile the inference layer underneath quietly quintupled.

T7: The plumbing is the play.
content_pack.substack_draft:
The serverless AI inference cycle is roughly eighteen months old, and Modal Labs just printed the clearest data point in it: revenue from $60 million to $300 million annualized in eight months.

The pattern maps to prior infrastructure cycles. In the early cloud era, AWS grew faster than most software companies built on top of it. In mobile, Qualcomm consistently printed better growth numbers than most app developers. The layer nobody talks about tends to monetize earlier than the one everyone watches. Modal sells serverless GPU compute for AI inference. Developers rent GPU access without managing servers. As the number of AI models in production grows, demand for inference compute grows with it regardless of which model wins the benchmark war.

I am not yet sure whether Modal specifically wins this category. Fireworks, Together, Baseten, and the hyperscalers are all competing for the same spending. But $60 million to $300 million in eight months is not a category signal. It is a product signal. Something is working, and the inference layer is worth tracking more carefully than most of the model releases consuming all the attention.

ideas.title: Apple Paid $1 Billion to Not Compete in AI
ideas.trend: iOS 27 Extensions confirmed at Google I/O (May 19) lets users choose Gemini, Claude, or Apple AI for Siri in Settings. TechCrunch reported the architecture in May. Apple paid Google $1B in January for Gemini to power Apple Foundation Models. WWDC is June 8.
ideas.consensus: Apple is executing a smart partnership strategy to add AI to its platform while maintaining privacy differentiation and ecosystem lock-in.
ideas.angle: Apple has conceded the frontier AI capability race and is turning iOS into a marketplace for other companies' AI. The company that built $3T through vertical integration is now renting its most important layer from a competitor. The $1B Google payment is rational — it costs one-tenth what building would cost — but it inverts Apple's 20-year competitive strategy and raises the question of whether the frame still commands a premium when the intelligence is rented.

content_pack.x_longform:
Apple built a $3 trillion company by owning its own silicon, its own software, and its own services. This year, it paid Google $1 billion to outsource the layer it cannot build.

The deal: a multiyear partnership signed in January where Google Gemini powers Apple Foundation Models and the next generation of Siri. Confirmed by a joint Apple-Google statement. TechCrunch reported this month that iOS 27 extends the model further with Extensions: users pick Gemini, Claude, or Apple's own system for Siri in Settings. Apple is building a marketplace inside its own OS where its AI competes against Google and Anthropic directly.

The math behind this decision is straightforward.

Staying at the frontier of AI requires concentrated compute investment at a scale Apple's profit structure cannot support. OpenAI spends $17 billion on compute this year, projecting $47 billion by 2028. Meta's 2026 capex hits $65 billion. Apple's entire R&D budget across hardware, software, silicon, services, and research runs to roughly $30 billion. Concentrating the majority of that into an AI compute race at negative operating margins breaks the business model.

The $1 billion Google payment is the rational alternative. Rent the capability at one-tenth the cost of building it. Wrap everything in privacy marketing that Google cannot credibly match. Charge premium hardware prices for the device that accesses the rented intelligence. Keep the 45% gross margin intact.

The historical parallel in Apple's own history is worth naming.

ARM designs the architecture Apple's chips run on. Apple licenses ARM, builds its own implementation on top, and uses vertical integration to outperform. The strategy works because ARM cannot build a phone.

Google can build a phone. Pixel exists. Android runs on two billion devices. The distinction matters because Apple's moat in this architecture depends on users choosing the frame over the intelligence inside it.

For twenty years, Apple's hardware was the intelligence. M-series chips, custom controllers, integrated sensors, software co-designed with silicon. The iOS 27 Extensions architecture inverts this. The intelligence is a commodity API call. Apple provides the frame.

The $1 billion is cheap. Whether users pay a premium for the frame when the intelligence is rented, that is the open question.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Apple's competitive story for twenty years has been total control of the stack. The company designed its own chips, wrote its own operating systems, built its own stores. The strategy created the most profitable technology business in history. In January, Apple paid Google $1 billion to power its next operating system's most important feature.

The logic is clear enough. Staying competitive in frontier AI requires compute investment at a scale that breaks Apple's profit model. OpenAI spends $17 billion on compute this year and projects $47 billion by 2028. Apple's entire R&D budget covers hardware, software, silicon, services, and research combined. The gap is not a priority problem. It is a math problem.

The iOS 27 Extensions architecture, reported by TechCrunch this month, takes this further. Users will choose between Gemini, Claude, or Apple's own model for Siri in Settings. Apple is building a marketplace where its AI competes against Google and Anthropic inside its own operating system.

I am not yet sure whether this damages Apple's long-term position. The $1 billion payment is cheap if it lets Apple maintain its hardware premium and 45% gross margins. The harder question is whether users eventually choose the phone for the AI rather than the AI adapting to the phone. If that shift happens, Apple's frame strategy stops working. I do not think anyone knows when or whether that shift arrives.
